purpose: Carboplatin is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat certain types of cancer, most commonly ovarian cancer, lung cancer, and head and neck cancers. It may be used alone or combined with other chemotherapy drugs. Your doctor chose this medicine because it helps stop cancer cells from growing and spreading.
how_it_works: Carboplatin works by attaching itself to the DNA inside cancer cells, which is like the cell's instruction manual. When the DNA gets damaged this way, the cancer cell can no longer make copies of itself and eventually dies. Healthy cells can also be affected, which is why some side effects occur, but cancer cells are much more sensitive to this damage.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include low blood cell counts (which can cause fatigue, increased risk of infection, or easy bruising and bleeding), nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, hair thinning, and numbness or tingling in the hands and feet. Kidney problems and hearing changes can also occur.
warnings: This medicine can seriously lower your blood counts, so you will need regular blood tests. Tell your doctor right away if you develop fever, chills, unusual bleeding, or signs of infection. Carboplatin can harm an unborn baby, so use reliable birth control during treatment. It can also cause allergic reactions — let your healthcare team know immediately if you feel flushing, rash, difficulty breathing, or dizziness during your infusion. Avoid live vaccines during treatment.
typical_dosing: Carboplatin is given through an IV (a drip into your vein) at a cancer clinic or hospital, usually once every 3 to 4 weeks. The exact dose is carefully calculated based on your kidney function and body size. Your oncology team will determine the right dose and schedule specifically for you.
